tasks.locator: Table 6, citalopram, fluoxetine and paroxetine rows; Results › MDMA › Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Second-hand summary. SSRIs lowered the rated and measured effects of MDMA. Citalopram (n=16): oceanic boundlessness about 60% lower, anxious ego dissolution about 63% lower (both p<.05), heart rate 12.3% lower at 60 minutes (p<.05), acute complaints about 46% lower (p<.01). Fluoxetine (n=8; Tancer and Johanson, 2006, not read): drug liking 31.2%, 'high' 47.6% and 'stimulated' 40.1% lower (all p<.05), heart rate 14.6% lower (p<.05). Paroxetine (n=12): liking about 62%, 'high' about 68% (p<.001), systolic pressure about 41% (p<.001) and heart rate about 42% lower (p<.05). The review summarizes this as 30 to about 80% lower subjective effects and, for physiological effects, about 6 to 14% lower (about 40 to 60% for paroxetine), and says that with fluoxetine and paroxetine, both strong CYP2D6 blockers, plasma MDMA was increased despite the attenuated effects (Table 6 gives no blood-level figure for fluoxetine). Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 1st paragraph; Table 5
tasks.extracted: No trial gave an SSRI or SNRI for months to people who take one as treatment: participants were young healthy adults given the medicine once or, rarely, for up to 14 days (the longest, escitalopram with psilocybin; for MDMA 3 to 11 days: paroxetine 3, fluoxetine 5 to 11), some by the less common intravenous route (citalopram). The authors write that no serious adverse effects of these combinations were observed in clinical trial settings and that, because the trials show smaller physiological effects, the odds of serotonin syndrome may be reduced at least with acute SSRI dosing (their inference, not tested); they also write that modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first.

tasks.locator: Table 6, duloxetine and reboxetine rows; Results › MDMA › Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Reboxetine and MDMA
tasks.extracted: Duloxetine (n=16) lowered nearly every effect of MDMA: 'any drug effect' 61.7%, drug liking 57.7% and closeness to others 83.1% (all p<.001), heart rate 57.4% and systolic pressure 63.5% (p<.001), and acute complaints 122.5% (p<.01; above 100% because, as the review says, complaints with duloxetine and MDMA were below the pre-drug baseline). Reboxetine (n=16) lowered 'any drug effect' by 20.7% (p<.01), closeness by 38.6% (p<.05), heart rate by 26.2% (p<.05) and systolic pressure by 46.5% (p<.001), but drug liking (-10.0%) and good drug effect (-15.2%) did not change significantly. Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

tasks.locator: Table 6, pharmacokinetic rows (Cmax, AUC) for each medicine; Results › MDMA, the paragraphs on bupropion, serotonin reuptake inhibitors, duloxetine and reboxetine
tasks.extracted: MDMA blood levels were higher with these medicines at the same time as effects were lower. Duloxetine: peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%, HMMA peak 40.5% lower. Reboxetine: peak +17.8%, exposure to 24 hours +8.1% (p<.05). Bupropion: peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak 75.9% lower. For comparison, carvedilol (+4.7%), clonidine (-2.9%), doxazosin (-1.6%) and methylphenidate (-3.5%) changed the peak by 5% or less, and memantine's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower. Table 6 has no blood-level row for citalopram or fluoxetine.

tasks.locator: Table 6, bupropion rows (Physiological; Circulating catecholamines; Subjective); Results › MDMA › Bupropion and MDMA; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Bupropion XR (n=16; taken for 7 days, with the amount stepped up, as listed in Table 5) did not blunt the rated effects: peak ratings of any drug effect, good effect, 'high', liking and 'stimulated' were 5.6 to 17.1% higher (no significance marks), and the areas under the rating curves over 8 hours were 36.7 to 46.1% higher for any drug effect, good effect, 'high' and liking (p<.05) and 34.0% higher for 'stimulated' (no mark), while heart rate was 38.7% lower (p<.001) and norepinephrine 65.6% lower (p<.05). The Results say bupropion significantly prolonged the positive mood effects of MDMA, and the Discussion that it prolonged the subjective effects and heightened the positive mood effects, and calls it plausible, without data, that bupropion with MDMA raises the risk of seizures, stimulant toxicity or serotonin syndrome because both are stimulants that can lower the seizure threshold and raise each other's blood levels. Its surveillance paragraph gives bupropion the highest unadjusted odds ratio of death of any antidepressant (2.82; see the claim on reports).

tasks.locator: Table 5; Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The 13 MDMA trials in Table 5 had 8 to 16 healthy adults each, nearly all double-blind counterbalanced crossovers; the medicine was given as a single dose or two doses within a day in 9 of the 13 and for 3 to 11 days in the other 4 (doxazosin, paroxetine, bupropion, fluoxetine). The Discussion says the trials came primarily from one laboratory group, that participants were young healthy adults, and that the studies are limited in their extrapolation to settings where medicines are taken daily for months or years. The percentage changes are the review's own calculation, and the review did not appraise the risk of bias of any included study.

tasks.locator: Results › Epidemiologic studies, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Surveillance study (Cohen et al., 2021, as summarized here): 946 unique reports of recreational ecstasy use in the US adverse-event database, 2000-2020 (mean age 28, 70.1% men). Adjusted odds ratios of a fatal outcome when a drug class was also reported: MDMA metabolites or analogs 8.71, muscle relaxants 8.17, anesthetics 7.13, amphetamines and stimulants 3.05, benzodiazepines 2.25, opioids 2.05, ethanol 2.03, antidepressants 1.62. Unadjusted odds ratios for single psychiatric medicines: bupropion 2.82, sertraline 2.36, venlafaxine 1.97, citalopram 1.92, olanzapine 1.86; all 18 reports with metoclopramide ended in death; risperidone and lithium odds ratios could not be calculated because there were no deaths. No intervals, numbers of deaths or denominators are given.

tasks.locator: Results › Epidemiologic studies, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Survey (Copeland et al., 2006, as summarized here): 216 adults who took ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug in the past 6 months (mean age 26, 63% men, mean 11 days of ecstasy use in 6 months). Of those who took antidepressants with ecstasy, 76% still felt euphoria, but rates of muscle rigidity (0% vs 45%), nystagmus (0% vs 33%), dizziness (19% vs 42%), headache (21% vs 62%) and heavy sweating (28% vs 53%) were higher; antidepressants were not analysed by class and included MAOIs. Group sizes and the order of the paired percentages are not stated.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Trends in case studies, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review's authors write that the blunted subjective effects of SSRIs may lead people to take escalating doses and so explain the higher odds of death in the surveillance data, and that benzodiazepines were associated with a higher adjusted odds ratio of death than antidepressants, opioids or alcohol; no data on amounts taken are given. The review found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA, and notes that the surveillance study concerns unregulated ecstasy use in non-clinical settings.
tasks.quote: may drive individuals to take escalating drug doses to achieve effects

tasks.locator: Table 6, haloperidol rows; Results › MDMA › Antipsychotics and MDMA
tasks.extracted: Haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously (n=14) did not change cardiovascular or thermogenic responses to MDMA or the startle response, according to the review, but made the state dysphoric: well-being about 31% lower (p<.05), state anxiety about 47% higher at 75 minutes (p<.01), oceanic boundlessness about 59% lower (p<.05). Table 6 lists heart rate 13.7%, systolic pressure 5.0%, diastolic pressure 2.3% and temperature 1.4% higher at 120 minutes, with no significance marks. Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

tasks.locator: Table 6, methylphenidate rows; Results › MDMA › Psychostimulants and MDMA; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Methylphenidate (n=16) delayed MDMA's time to peak by 45.8% (p<.05) without changing its peak (-3.5%) or exposure (+3.2%), raised heart rate 15.1% and the rate-pressure product 16.8% (both p<.001) and epinephrine 54.6% (p<.01), and raised acute and subacute complaints by 86.5% (p<.01) and 191.9% (p<.001), without adding psychoactive effects (any drug effect -1.4%).

tasks.locator: Table 6, adrenergic-agent rows (carvedilol, pindolol, clonidine, doxazosin); Results › MDMA › Adrenergic agents and MDMA, 2nd to 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Adrenergic agents (n=16 each): carvedilol lowered the heart-rate rise 79.0%, systolic 76.9% (both p<.001), diastolic 39.2% and temperature 42.0% (p<.05), as changes from baseline, with little change in ratings (any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%) while epinephrine (+204.3%) and norepinephrine (+789.7%) rose (both p<.001); pindolol (men) lowered peak heart rate by about 17.6% (p<.001), the global altered-state score by about 26.7% and oceanic boundlessness by about 31.9% (both p<.01) and 'dreaminess' by about 95% (p<.05), with no effect on mean arterial pressure or temperature; clonidine lowered mean arterial pressure by 4.5% by the area measure (p<.05; 27.2% at the peak, not marked significant) and norepinephrine; doxazosin lowered mean arterial pressure 6.8% at the peak (p<.05) but raised heart rate 9.6% (p<.05), and lowered the area of heightened-mood ratings (marked significant). Table 6 gives carvedilol's vital signs as changes from baseline and pindolol's and doxazosin's as raw peaks; values with a tilde were read off graphs. The Discussion calls the effect of clonidine and doxazosin on physiology minimal.

tasks.locator: Table 6, memantine rows; Results › MDMA › Memantine and MDMA
tasks.extracted: Memantine 20 mg (n=15) had no effect on MDMA-induced acute memory impairment or on mood, per the review. Table 6 lists, without significance marks, changes of 0.4 to 13.6% on memory tasks and 0.7 to 41.1% on mood scales, and a 'subjective high' rating 20.9% and 70.3% higher at 90 and 120 minutes; MDMA's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower.

tasks.locator: Table 4; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Table 4, which lists the controlled trials of psychiatric medicines by class, has no entry in its MDMA column for MAOIs, mood stabilizers (the class that includes lithium) or anxiolytics. The review says it found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA. Modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first; the review notes that tapering carries its own risks of relapse and discontinuation symptoms. Online communities were described as encouraging olanzapine as a way to end a distressing psychedelic experience; the review says it is unclear whether an atypical antipsychotic would be an appropriate approach.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Main text, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, limitations paragraph
tasks.extracted: Pooled analysis of eight double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies in 139 healthy people (70 men, 69 women): 7 CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, 19 intermediate and 113 extensive metabolizers (111 extensive in one Discussion comparison). Doses and study details are in a supplement that was not read; all seven poor metabolizers were in the high-dose group, and the authors state that an analysis of the high-dose group alone gave similar results (no figures are given in the text).

tasks.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph
tasks.extracted: Genotype altered MDMA levels only in the first 3 hours (absorption and distribution), not after: genotype main effect on peak MDMA F(2,136)=4.19, P=0.02, with higher peaks in poor than extensive metabolizers (P=0.049); area under the curve to 6 hours F(2,136)=5.25, P<0.01 (poor higher than extensive, P<0.01). Peak MDMA was 15% higher in poor metabolizers (abstract) and the mean ratio was 1.15 (7 poor against 111 extensive).

tasks.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend
tasks.extracted: The active metabolite MDA was higher and the inactive metabolite HMMA lower in poor metabolizers: peak MDA +50% (F(2,136)=8.82, P<0.01; area F=9.09, P<0.001); peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower (F(2,73)=3.50, P=0.03; area F=5.22, P<0.01), HMMA exposure to 6 hours about a quarter (24%) of extensive metabolizers'; MDMA to HMMA ratios higher in poor metabolizers (F(2,73)=10.98 and 10.08, P<0.001). The HMMA tests rest on fewer people than the MDMA and MDA tests: N=76 in the HMMA correlation and F tests with 73 error degrees of freedom, against 136 for MDMA and MDA.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Main text, 4th paragraph; Fig. 2 legend; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph
tasks.extracted: Poor metabolizers had faster early effects but not larger ones: systolic pressure rise greater than in intermediate (P=0.02) and extensive (P=0.01) metabolizers at 0.6 h (F(2,135)=3.50, P=0.03), 'any drug effect' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.05) and 'drug liking' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.001) and 1 h (P<0.01); maximal effects did not differ and there was no genotype effect on heart rate or temperature. The authors read the small, short-lived difference as the result of MDMA inhibiting CYP2D6 itself, turning all people into functional poor metabolizers within about 1 hour; they cite a model estimating a rise of only 36% in peak MDMA with no CYP2D6 function, and say medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 raised peak MDMA by 15 to 20% and exposure by 10 to 30%. They also note that poor metabolizers were not over-represented among ecstasy deaths (their reference 11), that severe or fatal toxicity with high MDMA exposure occurred with ritonavir, which blocks CYP2D6, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 (more than one enzyme system), and suggest that other enzymes and CYP3A4 inhibition may matter more than CYP2D6 genetics; no toxicity outcome was measured in the analysis.

tasks.locator: Table 6, pharmacokinetic rows (Cmax, AUC) for each medicine; Results › MDMA, the paragraphs on bupropion, serotonin reuptake inhibitors, duloxetine and reboxetine; Discussion › Pharmacokinetic interactions-MDMA, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Second-hand summary. Duloxetine: peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%; reboxetine: peak +17.8%; bupropion: peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak 75.9% lower; carvedilol, clonidine, doxazosin and methylphenidate changed the peak by 5% or less (memantine's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower). The Discussion names the strong enzyme blocker ritonavir as having caused significant toxicity with MDMA (Papaseit et al., 2012, not read).

tasks.locator: Introduction > MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Discussion > Pharmacogenetics and MDMA, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Second-hand summary of Schmid et al. (2016): people with only non-functional alleles (*3, *4, *5) had a peak MDMA level 19% higher and early exposure (to 6 hours) 25% higher than people with only *1 and *2 alleles, with faster onset and higher blood pressure; the review's 19% and 25% are for a narrower genotype comparison than the paper's headline 15% and are not reconciled with it (the paper's supplement was not read). Pooled trial data are said to show that effects follow plasma concentration and that higher CYP2D6 activity scores predict lower MDMA levels (Studerus et al., 2021, not read).

tasks.locator: MDMA CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibition and the phenocopying phenomenon, paragraph 1; Abstract; Concluding remarks, 2nd and 6th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Narrative review, second-hand. It says MDMA inactivates most liver CYP2D6 within about 2 hours and activity returns to its starting level only after at least 10 days (citing studies from 2008 and 2011), that phenocopying (the enzyme behaving as in a poor metabolizer whatever the genotype) was seen in 67% of male subjects in one study and 100% of females in another, and that the polymorphism and co-administered CYP2D6 inhibitors may have less impact on the risk of acute toxicity than previously thought. The 67% is 10 of 15 men in the 2008 study read for this library, whose first probe dose was at 4 hours and whose ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days; the 100% for women (2011) was not read. The Concluding remarks also say carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects, which the review's body does not support with numbers.

tasks.locator: Methods > Patients and study design, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Abstract (Methods)
tasks.extracted: Fourteen men took part: six in a pilot phase (two each at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and eight in a double-blind, randomized, Latin-square crossover of 75 mg MDMA, 125 mg MDMA, 40 mg amphetamine and placebo; all had used MDMA at least five times; in the second phase all were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers. The 150 mg volunteers had side effects that ruled out higher doses, and 50 mg was judged low.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (image; MDMA rows for 75 and 125 mg); Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: In the same eight men, 125 mg gave a higher dose-normalized exposure than 75 mg: peak 236.4 ug/L (SD 58.0) against 130.9 (38.6); AUC(0-24 h) 2623.7 (572.9) against 1331.5 (646.0); dose-normalized AUC 21.0 (4.6) against 17.8 (8.6); half-life 8.6 (3.2) against 7.7 (3.2) h. A paired t test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) gave P<0.03, and the 90% interval of the within-person ratio was -0.3 to 89.3%, so the authors judged the 125 mg dose not bioequivalent to the 75 mg dose scaled by dose. Editors' calculation: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the AUC.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (image; clearance columns); Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Urinary clearance of MDMA was roughly constant across doses (analysis of variance not significant) while non-renal clearance depended on dose (P<0.03) and, in the same eight men, was about halved at 125 mg (38.1 L/h) against 75 mg (74.0 L/h), which the authors read as impaired hepatic clearance; total clearance was 86.9 (SD 74.4) against 51.1 (14.1) L/h. The SDs of non-renal clearance are cut off at the edge of the table image.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (image; 50, 100 and 150 mg rows); Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Across the five doses (50 to 150 mg, a 3-fold range), with different men at each dose, the AUC(0-24 h) of MDMA ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug.h/L (more than 10-fold): two men at 50 mg had 100.1 and 813.9 ug.h/L, two men at 150 mg 5132.8 and 5232.0, with peak concentrations 441.9 and 486.9 ug/L at 150 mg against a mean of 236.4 at 125 mg. A Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) across the five doses was only marginal (P<0.1).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors name two explanations: saturation of MDMA metabolism (the simplest, which they say cannot be excluded) and inhibition of CYP2D6-mediated demethylenation by MDMA, and perhaps by its metabolite HMMA, citing in vitro work showing MDMA is both a substrate and an inhibitor of CYP2D6. Their stated limits: the observations were made retrospectively, the clinical studies were not designed to detect the phenomenon, and bias cannot be excluded because the same individuals were not tested at each dose level.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Conclusions)
tasks.extracted: The abstract concludes that the lack of proportionality, in a window of doses the authors call compatible with recreational use, is a more general phenomenon concerning the whole population independent of CYP2D6 genotype, and that relatively small increases in the dose ingested give disproportionate rises in plasma concentration, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity. Editors' reading: the dose comparison was made in eight men who were all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers, so independence from genotype was not tested, and no toxicity outcome was measured.
tasks.quote: subjects are more prone to develop acute toxicity

tasks.locator: Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph (also the following paragraph on limitations)
tasks.extracted: The authors read the small and short-lived difference between people with and without CYP2D6 function as the result of MDMA inhibiting CYP2D6 itself, citing a physiologically based model that estimates a rise of only 36% in peak MDMA with no CYP2D6 function; they note that other enzymes and CYP3A4 inhibition may matter more than CYP2D6 genetics.

tasks.locator: MDMA pharmacology and metabolic disposition, 4th paragraph; Drug-drug interactions, 1st paragraph; Concluding remarks, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Narrative review, second-hand. MDMA is both a substrate of CYP2D6 (O-demethylenation to HHMA, then methylation to HMMA) and a potent mechanism-based inhibitor; the review gives metabolic clearance as about 75% of MDMA plasma clearance, with about 30% of its metabolism regulated by CYP2D6 (citing the 2000 non-linear paper and a 2005 paroxetine-probe study), written elsewhere as less than 30% and, for both drugs, lower than 50%.

tasks.locator: 3. Results > 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph; Footnote 1
tasks.extracted: One infant in the MDMA-exposed group was diagnosed with Townes-Brocks syndrome, a rare genetic multiple-malformation syndrome of the gene SALL1, documented by genetic testing as a spontaneous (de novo) mutation; neither parent was a carrier. The authors say it would have occurred before conception and cannot be attributed specifically to maternal drug exposure; the mother had reported MDMA twice a month in the first trimester and none later, with cigarettes, alcohol and some cocaine. Results with and without this child did not differ. The paper does not report a count of other anomalies.

tasks.locator: 1. Introduction, 7th paragraph; 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The Introduction describes the 1999 series of 136 pregnancies as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk of congenital malformations and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies; the Discussion calls its 15.4% an increased risk, which echoes the letter's own summary. The letter reports a proportion (12 of 78 live births) compared informally with an unreferenced 2 to 3%, with no multiples printed, no adjusted analysis and no comparison group; it contains neither the 4 to 7 times nor the two-fold figure. Editors' calculation: 15.4% against an expected 2 to 3% is a ratio of about 5 to 8.

tasks.locator: 2. Methods > 2.1.1 Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.1.2 Measures of MDMA Exposure and Covariates, 1st paragraph; 2.1.2.1 Prenatal Levels of Drug Exposure, 1st paragraph; 2.1.4 Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Recruitment of pregnant women who had used recreational drugs through midwives, leaflets at prenatal clinics and advertisements in pregnancy magazines (ecstasy, tobacco, cannabis, alcohol and cocaine named as examples); 126 responded, 5 did not meet criteria, 25 did not come to the first visit, leaving 96; 82 infants were seen at about 1 month and 87 at 4 months. Women were classed as exposed if they said they used MDMA during pregnancy or in the month before (28); women who had used earlier but not then (32) and women who had never used were the comparison (68 in all). 62 women were interviewed during pregnancy and 24 after birth; use was by self-report with no biological check.

tasks.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 3rd to 7th paragraphs; Tables 2 and 4
tasks.extracted: Mean tablets a week for the 28 exposed women (Table 4): month before pregnancy 1.61 (SD 3.11), first trimester 0.82 (1.58), second 0.08 (0.38), third 0.006 (0.03); one woman used in the third trimester. Table 2: over pregnancy mean 0.6 (SD 1.1), median 0.13 (range 0.01 to 4.5). The text gives 3.2 tablets a week (SD 5.2) before pregnancy 'for those who used MDMA during pregnancy' and a mean total of 25 tablets over pregnancy and the month before (SD 43.7, range 0.45 to 180). Median split (0.14 a week): heavier 13 women, lighter 15; they differed mainly in the month before pregnancy (3.3 against 0.12 tablets a week, P<.007) and less in the first trimester (1.6 against 0.12, P<.12).

tasks.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Tables 1 to 3
tasks.extracted: The women who used MDMA were more likely to use cocaine (71% against 16% of women), cannabis (82% against 54%), tobacco (86% against 62%), amphetamine (18% against 3%), mushrooms (14% against none), LSD (11% against none) and ketamine (7% against none) in pregnancy, and used more alcohol (9.1 against 6.6 units a week; 96% against 91% of women); they had fewer previous births (parity 1.21 against 1.88) and higher drug-problem scores (DAST 7.7 against 4.6). The groups were similar in age, education, income, ethnicity and two intelligence subtests.

tasks.locator: 3. Results > 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 5
tasks.extracted: All births were singletons. No group difference in gestation (40.0 against 39.5 weeks), birth weight (3537 against 3344 g), prematurity (1 of 28 against 1 of 68), length or head circumference (the last two with many missing values). Exposed infants were more often male: 20 of 28 (71%) against 31 of 68 (46%), chi-square 5.32, P=0.02; odds ratio of a male birth 3.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 8.2, P<.02) after controlling for other drug differences. The authors state that they cannot establish whether the sex-ratio difference is caused by MDMA.

tasks.locator: 3. Results > 3.3 Neonatal Behavioral Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 6
tasks.extracted: NNNS at about 1 month (22 exposed, 60 comparison infants; mean age 33.6 days): no mean score differed (for example lethargy 3.14 against 2.63, P=.22; excitability 1.64 against 2.35, P=.15); trends in the score distributions for more lethargic behaviour (91% against 73%) and less hypertonicity (9% against 27%), both P<.069.

tasks.locator: 3. Results > 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 1st paragraph; Table 7
tasks.extracted: At 4 months (22 exposed, 65 comparison infants): Bayley mental index 99.1 (SD 6.4) against 98.6 (8.9), P=.80; psychomotor index 96.5 (10.0) against 94.3 (10.8), P=.40; behaviour-rating attention/arousal 71.2 against 70.9; Alberta motor scale percentile 50.4 against 45.8, P=.51, with 14% below the 10th percentile in both groups; behaviour-rating motor quality 58.9 (SD 20.7) against 74.1 (23.8), t -2.61, P=.009. After controlling for average alcohol exposure, MDMA still predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.21, P<.05); average tablets a week over pregnancy predicted it too (beta -.24, P<.042).

tasks.locator: 3. Results > 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 2nd paragraph; Table 8; 3.5 Other Drug Effects, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Three-group comparison at 4 months (none, lighter, heavier): behaviour-rating motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (F 3.6, P<.04); Alberta percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (F 3.8, P<.03); psychomotor index 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (P<.08); below the 10th percentile 14%, 0 and 27% (P<.18), so the lighter group scored above the unexposed on the psychomotor index and the Alberta percentile. Higher alcohol exposure predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.36, P<.005), and higher cannabis exposure poorer attention (beta -.28) and regulation (beta -.27) at 1 month (both P<.02).

tasks.locator: 4. Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs; Abstract; Highlights
tasks.extracted: Limitations the authors state: voluntary enrolment, self-reported use that may be unreliable, fetal exposure almost entirely in the first trimester, a small exposed sample, and fathers' use not asked. They conclude that the findings suggest risk to the developing child and warrant follow-up of the cohort to see whether the early motor differences persist or resolve. The abstract and highlights say exposed infants had poorer motor quality and lower milestone attainment, with a dose-response relationship; in the group comparison the Bayley psychomotor and Alberta scores did not differ.

tasks.extracted: SDLP model (18 drivers; stepwise selection among blood THC, breath alcohol, their product, speed limit, inverse curvature and subject; both concentrations modelled for the time of the drive from samples taken before and after it): blood THC b = 0.26 cm per µg/L (SE 0.07, p = 0.0004); breath alcohol b = 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L (SE 0.15, p = 0.0037); no THC-by-alcohol term was selected, and neither quadratic term. tasks.locator: Results › 3.1 Participants, 1st paragraph; Methods › 2.2 Study Design/Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion › 4.1 Strengths and limitations, 3rd to 5th paragraphs
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC4536116 (PMC HTML, author manuscript), read in the app's browser
tasks.extracted: Nineteen healthy adults drove (13 men, 6 women; ages 21–37; occasional cannabis smokers); participant 12 was excluded from all driving analyses after the fact, leaving 18. Six conditions (placebo, two strengths of vaporized cannabis, each with placebo or alcohol) in randomized order at least a week apart; a 45-minute night drive in a driving simulator began 0.5–1.3 hours after cannabis dosing. The authors note that participants know their driving is observed, that frequent smokers show tolerance to some effects, and that the model-selection procedure was used to describe the data; they do not regard use of a simulator rather than a road as a significant limitation. The paper reports no rating of how impaired participants felt.

tasks.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC4536116 (PMC HTML, author manuscript), read in the app's browser
tasks.extracted: The paper describes earlier work as inconsistent on whether cannabis and alcohol together act additively or synergistically: a simulator study found a lane-position increase only with the combination (Ronen 2010), another found separate effects and no interaction (Lenné 2010), and an on-road study found larger lane-position increases with low amounts of both combined than with either alone (Robbe 1998; Ramaekers 2000). Second-hand: these studies were not read for this library.

tasks.locator: Results › Primary and secondary analyses, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC3277079 (PMC HTML), read in the app's browser
tasks.extracted: In all studies that assessed cannabis in conjunction with alcohol, the estimated odds ratio for the combination was higher than for cannabis alone; the authors take this to suggest synergy, cite four sources and give no estimates. The comparison is with cannabis alone, so it does not separate an additive from a more-than-additive combination, since alcohol raises the odds on its own. The review's pooled estimates are for cannabis-only drivers (blood THC with no alcohol or other drug).

tasks.extracted: Nine studies of acute cannabis use in drivers (six culpability, three case-control; five fatal collisions, four non-fatal), cannabis-only drivers against drivers with none: pooled odds ratio 1.92 (95% CI 1.35–2.73), P = 0.0003, I-squared 81%; study estimates from 0.82 to 7.16; the authors rate the overall quality of evidence moderate. This pooled value was later revised downwards by re-extraction and adjustment (see the Rogeberg and Elvik anchors); the review is critically low on AMSTAR 2 on its study card.

tasks.extracted: Randomized, double-blind, four-arm crossover (placebo, ethanol, GHB, both; single fixed doses, study conditions) in healthy adults who drank lightly and had little GHB experience: 22 enrolled, 16 completed. Oxygen saturation fell with all three active conditions relative to placebo; the combination gave the largest drop, maximal mean change −2.12 ± 0.34 percentage points from baseline at 90 minutes, greater than placebo (P < 0.0001), GHB alone (P = 0.027) and ethanol alone (P = 0.013); saturation stayed below baseline for the 4 hours of monitoring with all three. Fig 2, read by eye (approximate): combination about −2.2 and GHB alone about −1.6 at 90 minutes. No interaction test, interval or baseline saturation is given.

tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC2766839 (PMC HTML, author manuscript), read in the app's browser
tasks.extracted: Vomiting on 8 study days (6 with the combination, 1 with GHB alone, 1 with ethanol alone) and 2 brief episodes of asymptomatic hypotension (systolic 71–73 mm Hg, under 15 minutes) after the combination; none needed treatment. Ethanol did not significantly change GHB pharmacokinetics (all P > 0.05; the study was powered to detect a 25% change in clearance). The authors describe a fall of about 2% in saturation as modest in absolute terms. Six of 22 enrolled did not complete.
